steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on AutoLTS, a deep learning framework that assesses cycling stress (level of traffic stress) of road segments from street-view images using contrastive learning and spatial post-processing. Motivate the problem, explain why plain image classification is not enough, outline the approach, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Cycling stress metrics and why the data they need is hard to get
- AutoLTS: street-view images, Toronto dataset, the LTS classes
- Why simple image classification falls short (three ignored structures)
- Two-step framework, contrastive learning and spatial post-processing
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Cycling stress metrics

  - metrics: level of traffic stress (LTS), bicycle level of service index; quantify perceived stress from built environment and motor traffic
  - predictive of cycling behaviors and accidents -> used for infrastructure planning, route recommendation
  - need high-resolution road network data: motor traffic speed, on-street parking locations, presence/type of cycling infrastructure per segment
  - collecting accurate, up-to-date data is hard -> limits broader application
- AutoLTS
  - deep learning framework, cycling stress of urban road networks from street-view images
  - timely, accurate, large-scale; images easy to get via Google StreetView API
  - dataset of 39,153 road segments, Toronto, Canada; focus on automating LTS
  - four classes LTS 1-4, cycling suitability of four types of cyclists; LTS 1 least stressful, LTS 4 most (Figure 1)
  - LTS used for connectivity and equity of cycling networks, evaluating cycling interventions during COVID-19
  - approach applies to any cycling stress metric
- Why not plain image classification
  - ignores i) causal relation road features -> LTS, ii) ordinal relations among labels, iii) spatial structure of road networks
  - dataset relatively small for computer vision (data collection, number of segments in a city)
  - ii) especially important: LTS1 predicted as LTS3 worse than as LTS2, since LTS2 = stress tolerance of most adults
  - may lead to redundant infrastructure on low-stress road or routes beyond most adults' tolerance
- Framework (Figure 2)
  - two-step: predict LTS-related road features from image + learn image representation; then combine embedding with predicted and available road features -> LTS
  - ii) contrastive learning: embedding clustered by LTS label, clusters positioned by ordinal relationship
  - iii) post-processing for spatial smoothness of road feature predictions
  - not on LTS directly: could smooth over important local patterns, needed e.g. for network design fixing disconnections between low-stress sub-networks
- Contributions
  - novel application: first dataset and first CV framework for automating cycling stress assessment
  - new methods: contrastive loss for ordinal classification generalizing supervised contrastive loss; spatial post-processing; both generalizable
  - strong performance: experiments on Toronto data; value of street-view images; effectiveness in real-world settings

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Safety and comfort concerns have been identified many times as major factors that stop people from cycling in cities around the world. Different metrics have been proposed to quantify the stress that cyclists perceive from the built environment and from motor traffic, such as the level of traffic stress (LTS) and the bicycle level of service index. These metrics predict cycling behaviors and accidents, so they have been used to support cycling infrastructure planning and route recommendation. But to calculate these metrics you usually need high-resolution road network data, such as the motor traffic speed, where the on-street parking is, and whether there is cycling infrastructure on each road segment and what type it is. In practice it is hard to collect accurate and up-to-date data, and this hinders the broader application of cycling stress assessment and of the tools that are built on it.

To deal with this challenge, we propose AutoLTS, which is a deep learning framework that assesses the cycling stress of urban road networks from street-view images. Since up-to-date street-view images are easy to access through the Google StreetView API, AutoLTS can make cycling stress assessments timely, accurate and large-scale. We use a dataset of 39,153 road segments collected in Toronto, Canada, and we focus on automating the calculation of the LTS metric. As shown in Figure 1, road segments are classified into four classes, LTS 1, 2, 3 and 4, which correspond to the cycling suitability of four types of cyclists. LTS 1 is the least stressful road and LTS 4 is the most stressful one. The LTS metric has been used to study the connectivity and the equity of urban cycling networks, and to evaluate cycling interventions during the COVID-19 pandemic. We use LTS for demonstration, but our approach applies to any cycling stress metric.

- Why not plain image classification
  - ignores i) causal relation road features -> LTS, ii) ordinal relations among labels, iii) spatial structure of road networks
  - dataset relatively small for computer vision -> must use i)-iii)
  - ii) especially important: LTS1 predicted as LTS3 worse than as LTS2 (LTS2 = stress tolerance of most adults); redundant infrastructure or routes beyond most adults' tolerance
- Framework (Figure 2)
  - two-step: road features + image representation, then combine embedding with predicted and available road features -> LTS
  - ii) contrastive learning, clusters ordered by label; iii) spatial smoothing of road feature predictions, not LTS (local patterns matter for network design)
- Contributions
  - novel application: first dataset and first CV framework for automating cycling stress assessment
  - new methods: ordinal contrastive loss generalizing supervised contrastive loss; spatial post-processing; both generalizable
  - strong performance: Toronto experiments; value of street-view images; effective in real-world settings

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Safety and comfort concerns have been identified many times as major factors that stop people from cycling in cities around the world. Different metrics have been proposed to quantify the stress that cyclists perceive from the built environment and from motor traffic, such as the level of traffic stress (LTS) and the bicycle level of service index. These metrics predict cycling behaviors and accidents, so they have been used to support cycling infrastructure planning and route recommendation. But to calculate these metrics you usually need high-resolution road network data, such as the motor traffic speed, where the on-street parking is, and whether there is cycling infrastructure on each road segment and what type it is. In practice it is hard to collect accurate and up-to-date data, and this hinders the broader application of cycling stress assessment and of the tools that are built on it.

To deal with this challenge, we propose AutoLTS, which is a deep learning framework that assesses the cycling stress of urban road networks from street-view images. Since up-to-date street-view images are easy to access through the Google StreetView API, AutoLTS can make cycling stress assessments timely, accurate and large-scale. We use a dataset of 39,153 road segments collected in Toronto, Canada, and we focus on automating the calculation of the LTS metric. As shown in Figure 1, road segments are classified into four classes, LTS 1, 2, 3 and 4, which correspond to the cycling suitability of four types of cyclists. LTS 1 is the least stressful road and LTS 4 is the most stressful one. The LTS metric has been used to study the connectivity and the equity of urban cycling networks, and to evaluate cycling interventions during the COVID-19 pandemic. We use LTS for demonstration, but our approach applies to any cycling stress metric.

If we formulate this task as a simple image classification problem, we may not use the training dataset to its full potential, because this ignores i) the causal relationship between road features and LTS, ii) the ordinal relationships among the LTS labels, and iii) the spatial structure of urban road networks. Our dataset is relatively small for a computer vision task, because of the practical data collection challenge and because a city only has so many road segments, so it is critical to use i)–iii) to improve the prediction performance. Item ii) is particularly important, because misclassifications between different pairs of LTS labels mean different things in practice. For example, predicting an LTS1 road as LTS3 is worse than predicting it as LTS2, because LTS2 corresponds to the cycling stress tolerance of most adults. The first kind of error may lead to redundant cycling infrastructure on a low-stress road and or to recommended cycling routes that are beyond the stress tolerance of most adults.

To capture i), we formulate the LTS assessment as a two-step learning task, as illustrated in Figure 2. First we predict road features related to LTS from the input image and learn high-quality representations of the image. Then we combine the image embedding with the predicted and available road features to make the final LTS prediction. With this two-step framework we can capture ii) with contrastive learning and iii) with a spatial post-processing technique. For ii), we propose a contrastive learning approach that learns an image embedding space where the images are clustered by their LTS labels and the clusters are positioned according to the ordinal relationship among the labels. For iii), we develop a post-processing technique that enforces spatial smoothness on the road feature predictions. We do not enforce spatial smoothness on the LTS predictions directly, because it may smooth over important local patterns, and these patterns are critical for downstream applications such as cycling network design, which aims to fix the disconnections between low-stress sub-networks. Our contributions are the following.

- 1. A novel application. We introduce the first dataset and the first computer vision framework for automating cycling stress assessment.

- 2. New methodologies. We propose a new contrastive loss for ordinal classification which generalizes the supervised contrastive loss. We also develop a post-processing technique that adjusts the road feature predictions by considering the spatial structure of the road network. Both of them can be easily generalized to other tasks.

- 3. Strong performance. We run comprehensive experiments with a dataset collected in Toronto, Canada, and we show i) the value of street-view images for cycling stress assessment, and ii) that our approach is effective in a wide range of real-world settings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Safety and comfort concerns have been repeatedly identified as major factors that inhibit cycling uptake in cities around the world. A range of metrics, such as the level of traffic stress (LTS) [1,2] and the bicycle level of service index [3], have been proposed to quantify cyclists' perceived stress imposed by the built environment and motor traffic. These metrics are predictive of cycling behaviors [4,5] and accidents [6], and have thus been applied to support cycling infrastructure planning [7,8,9] and route recommendation [6,10]. However, calculating these metrics typically requires high-resolution road network data, such as motor traffic speed, the locations of on-street parking, and the presence and type of cycling infrastructure on each road segment. The practical challenge of collecting accurate and up-to-date data hinders the broader application of cycling stress assessment and of the tools built on it.

To tackle this challenge, we propose AutoLTS, a deep learning framework for assessing the cycling stress of urban road networks based on street-view images. Because up-to-date street-view images are easy to access via the Google StreetView API, AutoLTS can facilitate timely, accurate, and large-scale assessments of cycling stress. Using a dataset of 39,153 road segments collected in Toronto, Canada, we focus on automating the calculation of the LTS metric. As shown in Figure 1, road segments are classified into four classes, i.e., LTS 1, 2, 3 and 4 [11], corresponding to the cycling suitability of four types of cyclists, where LTS 1 is the least stressful road and LTS 4 the most stressful. This metric has been used to investigate the connectivity [7,12] and equity [13] of urban cycling networks and to evaluate cycling interventions during the COVID-19 pandemic [14]. While we focus on LTS for demonstration, our approach applies to any cycling stress metric.

Formulating this task as a simple image classification problem may not use the training dataset to its full potential, as it ignores i) the causal relationship between road features and LTS, ii) the ordinal relationships among LTS labels, and iii) the spatial structure of urban road networks. Leveraging i)–iii) is critical for prediction performance, since our dataset, limited by the practical data collection challenge and by the number of road segments in a city, is relatively small for a computer vision task. Item ii) is particularly important because misclassifications between different pairs of LTS labels have different empirical meanings. For example, predicting an LTS1 road as LTS3 is worse than predicting it as LTS2, because LTS2 corresponds to the cycling stress tolerance of most adults [1]. The former may lead to redundant cycling infrastructure on a low-stress road and or to recommended cycling routes that exceed most adults' stress tolerance.

As illustrated in Figure 2, we capture i) by formulating LTS assessment as a two-step learning task. We first predict LTS-related road features from the input image and learn high-quality representations of the image. We then combine the image embedding with the predicted and available road features to produce the final LTS prediction. This two-step framework allows us to capture ii) and iii) via contrastive learning and a spatial post-processing technique, respectively. To address ii), we propose a contrastive learning approach that learns an image embedding space in which images are clustered by their LTS labels and the clusters are positioned according to the ordinal relationship among these labels. To tackle iii), we develop a post-processing technique that enforces spatial smoothness in road feature predictions. We choose not to enforce spatial smoothness directly in LTS predictions, as this may smooth over important local patterns that are critical for downstream applications such as cycling network design, which aims to fix disconnections between low-stress sub-networks. Our contributions are summarized below.

- 1. A novel application. We introduce the first dataset and the first computer vision framework for automating cycling stress assessment.

- 2. New methodologies. We propose a new contrastive loss for ordinal classification that generalizes the supervised contrastive loss [15]. We also develop a post-processing technique that adjusts road feature predictions based on the spatial structure of the road network. Both can easily be generalized to other tasks.

- 3. Strong performance. Through comprehensive experiments on a dataset collected in Toronto, Canada, we demonstrate i) the value of street-view images for cycling stress assessment, and ii) the effectiveness of our approach across a wide range of real-world settings.
